The motel room smelled like other people's cigarettes. Martin didn't remember checking in, so he checked the notes taped above the bed instead. FIND R.M. AVENGE HER. He dialed the number written on his palm in ballpoint and told the man on the other end everything about Elias Prine—the psychosomatic memory loss he'd ruled fraudulent, the denied claim, the diabetic wife who'd tested her husband's forgetting with syringe after syringe until she overdosed on his blank kindness. He told it like a confession that belonged to someone else.

Photographs covered the wall behind him: his wife's face, a stranger dead on tile, initials burned into a Polaroid border. He didn't remember taking most of them. He trusted them anyway, because trust was cheaper than memory.

Earlier—though he wouldn't have called it earlier, since for him there was no ladder of days, only a flat present—he'd stood in a field with a hairbrush and a stack of paperback books, burning what was left of a woman he mourned freshly every single time, as if grief itself refused to scar over.

Before that, tile under his knees, glass in the shower door, a man's hand on his throat and then not. He'd killed one intruder in his own bathroom and taken a blow that erased the machinery of remembering. His wife had not survived what came after; the second man, the one marked only R.M. in his own handwriting, had.

On the phone, the caller gave him a name: Gil Marsh, a dealer, a location. Martin thanked a stranger for the shape of his own revenge.

He found Gil in a basement that smelled of concrete and rot, beat him against a pipe, and closed a rope around his throat until the man's mouth stopped forming words except one: *Elias*. Martin photographed the body without understanding the name, then wore the dead man's suit out into the night and drove off in his car, the leather still warm.

Roy found him there, badge loose in his coat, and said the thing Martin refused to hold: that Gil was innocent, that the real killer had already died a year ago under Martin's own hands, that Roy himself had helped him do it, that the story of Prine's vanished memory was not a case file—it was Martin's face in the mirror. Martin burned the photographs of Gil instead of believing him, wrote HE IS LYING TO YOU across Roy's picture, and copied the license plate from Roy's sedan onto a scrap of paper like a verdict.

At the parlour the needle bit into his thigh, adding a sixth fact to a body already covered in instructions to itself.

At her bar, Corinne looked at the dead man's watch on a stranger's wrist, the car in the lot, and served him a beer her staff had spat into, smiling the whole time.

Later, in her kitchen, she hid every pen in the house, needled him until his hand rose, then came home late with a bruise blooming under one eye and Vance's name in her mouth like a gift.

Martin found Vance in a motel bathroom that could have been any bathroom, beat him until the tile went red, and drove him to the town line at gunpoint, feeling righteous in a way that had no memory to correct it.

Corinne ran the plate through a cousin at the registry and handed him a printout with a name circled twice: Roy Mercer.

Martin lured him to the derelict building where Gil had died, the smell of old rope still faint in the corners, and shot him once, cleanly, in the head, then photographed the body the way he photographed everything—so that tomorrow, forgetting again, he could believe he had finally, finally been right.

The heart arrived in a cooler, though Aaron never let himself picture the cooler, only the fact of the heart, sudden and unearned, beating in a chest that had nearly quit.

Della kept a photograph of Aaron from before—healthier, laughing at something out of frame—propped on her dresser, and she looked at it while he slept beside her in the hospital's family room, thinking about the vials in the freezer downtown, thinking that a man who might die owed her a child before he did. She never got the chance to press him again after he left. He told her flatly, later, that he didn't want it, the child she'd been trying so hard to make happen, and she never understood whether that refusal came from the same fear that had made her ask in the first place.

Wes Tarrow told his Bible study group once that God had given him a second chance nobody deserved, and the boys on his baseball team believed him more than his wife did. Nita watched him pray over breakfast and flinch at nothing, and she waited for the temper she still remembered from before his faith to surface again. It did, in its way, though not as a fist—only as a wheel jerking, a bumper meeting flesh, and then the terrible arithmetic of turning back versus driving on. He turned back. Then he didn't stop again until he was three states from the crossing.

Lena had been clean four years when the officer's face told her everything before his mouth did. Doug and the girls, gone, all three, and the heart that had been beating in her husband's chest kept beating somewhere else, in someone else, though she wouldn't know that yet. She went back to the powder like returning to an old address. She was thorough about the ruin she made of herself, the way she'd once been thorough about staying sober.

Wes walked into a station on his own legs and said what he'd done, and they sent him back to a cell he thought his faith had freed him from forever.

Aaron, alive in a way he hadn't let himself expect, could not stop pressing his hand to his own sternum, feeling the beat that was not his history. He hired a man to find out whose it had been. The investigator brought him a name, an address, a woman swimming laps alone in the mornings at a chlorine-bright municipal pool.

He arranged to be there. He arranged to be noticed. It became, before either of them named it, an affair conducted in the shorthand of grief.

He told her the truth in a motel room that wasn't the motel yet, and she threw a lamp at him, then let him back into her bed within the week, because the heart under his hand was somehow still Doug's heart, and she could not stop touching what remained of her husband.

Wes, out early on good behavior, left Nita a note and left his faith folded up somewhere behind him, and took a job changing sheets at a motel off a highway that led nowhere he'd been before.

Lena said his name like a curse and told Aaron to end it, and Aaron, who had never held a gun before that week, bought one and found the motel through means he didn't examine too closely.

He found Wes behind the ice machine and could not do what he'd driven there to do. He shot him once, badly, and told him to run before Wes could ask why he hadn't run himself.

Wes did not run far. He came to their door instead, bleeding through a shirt, and asked Aaron to finish it properly this time. Aaron looked at the gun, then at his own chest, and turned it there instead.

At the hospital the borrowed heart gave out for good, undoing itself the way it had once been undone in Doug. Wes went home, finally, to whatever was left of Nita. Lena went home alone, carrying, without yet knowing the shape of it, one more thing that didn't belong to her and wouldn't leave.

THE WATCH

The old soldier's hands trembled as he pressed the gold watch into the boy's palm. "Your father carried this through every year they held him," he said. "Never sold it, never traded it, even when it might've bought him a softer bed." The boy, who would grow up to be called Denny, closed his fist around it and felt the weight of something he didn't yet understand.

Years later, in a motel room with peeling wallpaper, Denny sat across from Marielle as she confessed she'd left the watch behind in his apartment. He didn't shout. He just stared at the ceiling for a long moment, the fight still fresh on his knuckles, blood he hadn't washed off yet drying at his hairline. "I have to go back," he said, and she knew better than to argue.

He'd won that fight the way his father would have wanted, except he'd been paid to lose it. Otis had put good money on the fifth round, and Denny had taken the money and then decided, in the ring, under the lights, that he wasn't going to be anybody's dive. He beat his opponent to death instead, and left in a taxi with his heart going like a hammer.

So he returned to his apartment for the one object that connected him to his father, and found instead Rollo, the hitman who'd been sent to collect on Otis's behalf, standing in his kitchen. There was a submachine gun on the counter. Denny didn't remember deciding to pick it up. He remembered the noise, and Rollo folding down like a marionette with its strings cut.

Before that, in the life Rollo had been living, there had been a night at a themed diner with Nadia, Otis's wife, the two of them winning a dance contest under paper streamers, laughing like people who didn't know what came next. There had been her hand reaching for his jacket pocket afterward, finding the little bag he'd bought off his dealer Kip, snorting it before he could stop her, and the terror of her going still on the dealer's carpet, the needle of adrenaline they drove into her chest to bring her back gasping.

There had been, earlier still, the job that started it all: Rollo and Marcus driving across town arguing about what a Quarter Pounder was called in France, then standing in a corridor arguing about whether a foot massage justified a killing, and finally the killing itself — Marcus reciting scripture like a man clearing his throat before a toast, then both of them putting bullets into a young double-crosser named Tobin, taking the briefcase Otis wanted so badly. The fourth man in the bathroom had emptied his revolver and hit nothing, which Marcus took as proof of God. Later, in the car, Rollo's gun went off by accident and took the head off a man named Del who hadn't done anything except sit in the wrong seat.

They'd cleaned the car at Warren's house, changed their bloody clothes, and gone on with the job as if nothing unusual had happened, stopping at a diner where two amateur robbers decided, mid-breakfast, to hold the place up. Marcus had talked the nervous one down, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase tucked at his feet the whole time, and let them walk out into the morning like it was nothing.

They'd delivered that briefcase to Otis at his bar, the same night Otis was paying Denny to take the dive that never came.

After Denny killed Rollo, he went looking for Marielle, but found Otis first — their cars colliding in the street, the two of them dragged into a pawnshop basement by men with rope and worse intentions. Denny broke his bindings, found a sword mounted crookedly on the wall, and used it while one of the captors was on top of Otis. Afterward Otis, bleeding, called it even, so long as Denny left the city forever.

He collected Marielle from the motel. They took a motorcycle from the pawnshop's back room. The watch was in his pocket, ticking against his hip as they rode out past the last streetlights, toward wherever roads like that one go.

Tobias woke on a train he didn't remember boarding, on a morning he couldn't account for. He'd skipped work on an impulse with no shape to it, some undertow pulling him toward the coast, and now the rail line was running out beneath frost-white fields toward the sea.

He hadn't wanted the memories to go at first. He'd wanted them gone before that. It's easier to explain backward.

The night before, in his flat, Dell and Peck had run the machine while Tobias watched his own life dissolve from the inside. The most recent memories went first—the dent in his car, Ivy's voice thick with gin, the door slamming for the last time. Good riddance, he'd thought, watching recrimination burn off like fog. Then came the noodle house, the ice on the river, the drive-in with the windows fogged from breath and laughter, and something in him rebelled. He tried to smuggle her into memories she'd never touched—birthdays, a childhood kitchen—hiding her where the technicians wouldn't think to erase.

Down the hall, Dell and Rosa had gotten high on his bed and lost the thread entirely, the map of his mind sliding sideways while no one watched the clock.

The train slowed at the coast station. Tobias walked down through the frozen dunes not knowing why his legs carried him there, and there she was — a woman on the sand, feet bare despite the cold, looking at the water like she was waiting for someone she couldn't name either.

Earlier, Dr. Hallam had arrived at the flat to fix the failing map, and Rosa, giddy and reckless, had kissed him — only to be told by his wife, arriving unannounced, that this had already happened once, and been erased, and here they were again, doomed to repeat what neither of them could remember choosing.

Ivy turned when Tobias's shadow crossed the sand. Neither said anything about who they were. They only felt the old current between them, unlabeled now, clean.

Before that, days earlier, Tobias had sat in Hallam's office demanding the same erasure Ivy had bought herself after Nina and Grady showed him the clinic's form letter — the one that confirmed what he'd suspected in the bookshop, watching Ivy laugh at something Peck said, her eyes empty of him entirely, as though he were a stranger asking after directions.

He and Ivy walked back to the road together now, strangers with a decade of unspoken gravity between them, and she asked if he wanted a ride into the city. He said yes.

Before the bookshop, before the form letter, there had been the boxing up: every sweater, matchbook, and dented earring that still held her, sorted into crates for the clinic's technicians to read like a map of wounds. Peck had pocketed a few mementos that night — a scarf, a photograph — meaning to use them on Ivy later, though no one knew that yet.

In her flat above the city that same afternoon, she poured two glasses of wine and put on a stack of tapes she'd found in a drawer she didn't remember filling. Their own voices came out of the speakers, young and furious, tearing each other apart over money, over silence, over the dent in a car neither of them owned anymore. Ivy ran to the bathroom and locked the door. When she came out her makeup was ruined and her voice was steady.

"We could try again," she said. "Knowing all that."

Weeks later, Rosa quit the clinic in disgust and mailed every patient their files and session tapes, unable to carry the weight of erasures nobody consented to twice.

And in the last surviving memory, before all of it, in an empty house on the shore where two teenagers had once broken a window to get out of the rain, Tobias and Ivy stood in the doorway saying goodbye for what neither of them yet knew was not forever.

"Meet me at the beach," she told him.

He did.

Danny Roarke lay on the concrete floor of the warehouse with a bullet in his gut and another man's gun still smoking six feet away, and while the blood pooled warm beneath him he found himself thinking, absurdly, of Pruitt's voice in a parked car three months ago, coaching him.

Say it slower, Pruitt had told him. Nobody remembers a story fast. You tell it like you're pulling it up out of the mud. Danny had practiced the anecdote about the drug bust in the men's room until the lie sat in his mouth like a real memory, until he could taste the bleach smell of that toilet even though he'd invented it whole. He'd performed it for Bram, for Cal, for a silent man named Ash, in the back room of a bar that smelled of fryer oil, and when he finished Bram had nodded once and said welcome aboard, Mr. Elm.

That had been the beginning of it, before all this.

Ren Vasco had walked out through the gates of the prison not long after that, blinking in daylight he hadn't earned honestly, and gone straight to Bram and Cal to collect what he was owed for years of silence. They'd shaken his hand like a debt paid.

At breakfast, before the job, the whole crew had argued — stupidly, warmly — about whether a pop song on the radio was really about heartbreak or about something else entirely, and whether the waitress refilling their coffee deserved a bigger tip than Birch wanted to leave. Bram had laughed and slid the tree names across the table like poker chips. Birch had objected loudest. I'm not being Mr. Birch, he'd said. Nobody's ever been shot for being called Birch, Cal had told him, and everybody had laughed, not knowing.

Now Danny lay on the warehouse floor with none of that laughter left anywhere in the building.

The job had collapsed in under a minute — alarms, sirens, everything gone wrong at once — and Ash had put the car through police cordon with the wheel fighting him and his gun out the window the whole way. Danny had gone out the other door on foot, into a stranger's car, and the driver, terrified, had put a bullet in his stomach before Danny put two into him.

Ash had carried him after that, screaming, into the warehouse, cradling him on the concrete and swearing, swearing, you are not going to die, not like this, not you.

Birch had come next, ranting that the whole job stank of an informer, that someone inside had sold them, before slipping out to bury the diamonds somewhere in the weeds outside.

Then Cedar had strolled in smiling, and popped his trunk to show them a bound, gagged patrolman named Doyle folded in the back like luggage.

Left alone with him, Cedar had turned on the radio, some oldie crackling through static, and danced while he worked — a knife, an ear, a can of petrol he upended over the officer's shaking body, laughing at nothing.

Danny had shot him from the floor, one round, clean, and told the sobbing cop the truth: I'm police. They're outside. They're waiting for Bram.

Cal walked in on the tail end of that confession, listened to Danny's account of what Cedar had done, and put a bullet in Doyle's skull without changing his expression.

Then Bram, finally, filling the doorway, looking at Danny with an old grief already settled into his face, and said the word informer like a verdict. Ash hadn't believed it — turned his gun on Bram instead, screaming denial — and the room became gunfire, three men falling in a triangle of noise, until only Ash and Danny were left breathing on the cold floor.

I'm a cop, Danny said again, quieter this time, blood in his teeth.

Ash's face didn't change. He raised the gun as the doors burst open and light and shouting poured in, and fired once before the police cut him down where he knelt.

The workmen found the sled first, before anything else made sense of it. It was a small thing, painted red once, the name BLUEBELL scratched into its runner in a boy's uneven hand, and they were shoveling it toward the furnace at Silvermount along with the rest of the debris when Nash arrived to ask his question.

He had been sent by his editor to find out what a dying man's last word meant. It seemed a small assignment. Emmett Rusk, newspaper king, twice-married, once a candidate for governor, had died alone in the unfinished palace he'd built and abandoned, and the newsreels had already run their obituaries — the mining money, the deed, the Clarion, the failed campaign, the second wife's ruined career — closing, always, on the mystery of that single murmured word, unexplained.

Nash went first to the nightclub by the sea, because that was where they said Nora Kell had gone to disappear. He found her drunk at a corner table, and she looked at him with an expression that had nothing left in it to give away, and told him to leave before he'd finished his sentence.

So he went instead to paper. He read the old banker Barrow's memoir, a vain and self-serving book, but in it was the story of a boy on a sled who'd once driven the wind out of him rather than be taken east to a fortune, and had been taken anyway. He talked to Marsh, who remembered the young man who'd walked into a failing paper and printed his principles on the front page like a boast, who'd hired away a rival's whole staff and thrown a party with a brass band just to prove he could. He talked to Devlin, who'd loved him once as a friend does, who remembered the marriage to Adele curdling into two people reading newspapers across a silent breakfast table, remembered the mistress in the rented rooms, the party boss who'd dragged the wife there to threaten exposure and the refusal that cost Emmett the governorship, cost him Adele, cost him Devlin's patience until Devlin asked to be sent to another city rather than watch what came next.

What came next, Devlin told him with a bitterness that hadn't faded, was Nora herself — married in haste, put on a stage she had no voice for, humiliated before an audience that came only to watch her fail. Devlin, drunk, had started the review that damned her. Emmett had finished it himself, printed it, and fired his oldest friend for the sin of having begun it.

Colm the butler remembered what came after that: the poison she swallowed rather than sing again, and Emmett's strange, too-late mercy in finally letting her stop. He remembered the half-built house at Silvermount where Emmett shut her away among unfinished halls, where she sat for hours over jigsaw puzzles in rooms too large for any voice to fill. He remembered a picnic on the beach that ended in silence and a quarrel, and Nora packing a single case and going.

And Colm remembered, though he hadn't understood it until now, the night Emmett tore apart her abandoned bedroom, flinging aside dresses and letters, and found at the bottom of a trunk a glass snow globe — a tiny sled inside it, red, motionless in its frozen flurry — and how he had gone still and said one word, "Bluebell," before carrying it past the mirrored corridors to the room where he would die holding it.

Nash wrote his story, but he did not write an answer, because there wasn't one. A man's whole noisy life — the mines, the marriages, the newspapers, the ruined voice, the empty palace — could not be folded into a single word any more than a life could be folded into a single scene. Bluebell was a sled a boy had ridden into a banker's stomach rather than leave his mother's kitchen; it was also, perhaps, nothing but a name on a toy he'd once loved and lost, glimpsed again by accident in a house full of things he had ruined.

The furnace took the real sled without ceremony, runners and paint and all, while Nash stood watching the smoke go up, no closer to certainty than the dead man's newsreel had left him, and understood at last that this, too, was the truest thing he could print.

The old man's flat overlooked the street, and through the window the blue lights turned the wet cobbles into something almost beautiful. "Nothing survives time," he said to the younger man beside him, gesturing at the scene below as though it proved his point. "Not love, not vengeance. Only the shape of things repeating."

Below, the police were dragging two handcuffed men out of the club called the Pit, their shirts torn, their faces slack with the particular exhaustion of men who have already done the worst thing they are capable of that night.

Not long before, Jonah had swung a fire extinguisher into a stranger's face while the real Adder stood a few feet away, arms folded, watching with the calm of a man who has seen this before and knows he will not be the one who pays for it.

Not long before that, Cort had seized the wrong man in the crowded dark of the club, certain in his fury, and heard the man's arm snap under his own hands, the sound thin and wrong beneath the music.

Not long before that, two men on the street had leaned in close to Cort and Jonah, offering a name for money, tilting their heads toward the doorway of the Pit like men selling directions to a cathedral.

Not long before that, Cort and Jonah had come stumbling out of the party's noise and light to find Lise being lifted into an ambulance, her face unrecognizable, her hands very still.

Not long before that, in the underpass she had taken to avoid the traffic, a man known as the Adder had raped Lise and beaten her head against the concrete while, at the far end of the tunnel, a passer-by paused, looked, and then walked quickly the other way.

Not long before that, Lise had walked into that same underpass and found the Adder beating a girl who flinched at every blow, the fluorescent light stuttering above them both.

Not long before that, disgusted, Lise had left the party alone, stepping past Cort as he laughed too loudly with a woman who wasn't her, his pupils blown wide, a rolled note still pinched between two fingers.

Not long before that, the three of them—Lise, Cort, Jonah—had ridden the underground together, arguing cheerfully about sex, about drinking, about nothing, the carriage rattling under the river while Cort promised he'd only have one drink at the party.

Earlier still, before any of that, Lise had sat in a park among children shrieking through sprinklers, a paperback open on her knee, one hand resting lightly on her stomach as though listening for something.

Before that, alone in the flat with the tap still running in the bathroom, she had watched the second line resolve itself on the little plastic stick, and had sat down slowly on the edge of the bathtub.

And longest ago of all, in the gray hour before waking, she had lain in bed with Cort, his arm heavy across her, describing the tunnel from her dream—red-walled, narrowing, always the same—while he teased her about Jonah, about old boyfriends, about nothing, the two of them laughing under the blankets as if there were nothing else in the world to fear.

"You see," the old man said, letting the curtain fall back across the window, "it doesn't matter which end you start from. The shape's already there. Whatever they think they're walking into, they walked out of it years ago." The younger man said nothing. Below, the ambulance had long since gone, and the street had gone quiet, and the lights in the club had begun, one by one, to go dark.

I hold hands with Ada Vey at a window on the top floor of a building I helped mine, and below us the city is already leaning, and she says nothing because there is nothing left to negotiate. That comes later. Let me back up.

I couldn't sleep. Not in the ordinary sense—my body would lie down and my eyes would close and nothing behind them would go dark. A specialist told me insomnia like mine is often about control, about a refusal to let go of the wheel even in the one hour a day nobody's watching. What worked, in the end, wasn't medication. It was crying. Specifically, crying in support groups for diseases I did not have. Testicular cancer. Blood parasites. A rare bone-wasting condition whose name I can't spell. I'd sit in a circle of folding chairs and let somebody else's grief pour into me until I broke, and then I'd sleep like the dead.

Ada Vey ruined that. She started showing up to the same groups, and her crying was so obviously performed, so theatrical, that it made mine feel like a lie too. I stopped sleeping again.

On a business flight not long after, I sat beside a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, who talked the whole flight about fat and lye and the alchemy of turning waste into product. I took his card because it seemed rude not to.

My apartment exploded a week later—gas line, they said, though nothing about it ever added up—and every piece of catalogue furniture I owned went up with it. I called the only number I had. Rex met me at a derelict house on the edge of the industrial district and told me I could stay.

Outside a bar one night he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. He hit back. We ended up in the car park bleeding into the gravel, and something about it felt like the first honest thing I'd done in years. It became weekly. Then it became a basement. Then it became a club with rules nobody remembers writing, and more men kept finding their way down the stairs.

Ada overdosed and Rex brought her back to the house on his shoulder, and after that the two of them were a loud, wet, inescapable thing I had to live beside. Rex, meanwhile, had a business again—rendering fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap, selling it back to department stores for eighty dollars a bar, laughing about the poetry of it.

He burned my hand with lye once and held it there when I tried to leave my body the way I'd learned to leave it in those groups. "Stay," he said. "Stay in this."

I blackmailed my employer with my own ruined face, and they paid me to disappear.

The club became an organization. Rex called it Havoc. Shaved heads filled the house, took orders, went out at night to break things that belonged to men who'd never break anything themselves.

Then Rex steered a car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and vanished from the wreck before I could reach him.

A man named Ogden was shot on an operation I hadn't approved, and I decided to end it. Havoc had metastasized. I went city to city trying to shut down chapters I hadn't known existed and found them everywhere, identical, and men greeting me by his name.

I am Rex Marrow. He has been living the nights I couldn't hold onto. Ada confirmed it without flinching—she'd been sleeping with the man in front of her the whole time.

Then I learned what he'd built toward: the towers of the debt-record companies, mined floor by floor. I went in to defuse it. He met me on a stairwell and beat me down it, and at the bottom I put the gun in my own mouth, angled it through my cheek, and fired to kill only him.

The recruits brought Ada to me at the window as the charges went off in sequence below, glass breathing out of every floor, and she took my hand, and neither of us said the thing there was no longer any use in saying.

Solly Two Coats had always liked the smell of church candles, which was why the pilgrim robes worked so well. He and his crew walked out of the diamond house in the northern port with a stone the size of a knuckle and the swagger of men who had just prayed for it.

Marv called from overseas before the boat had even left dock. "Bring it straight to me," he said. "Don't stop, don't sell, don't breathe on it wrong."

That was easier said than done. In the city, Grigor the Nail was already talking business — he told Solly, friendly as anything, about a bookmaker's worth a look, and in the same breath told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that the same bookmaker's was ripe for the taking. Grigor liked to plant two seeds in one row and see which one grew.

Around the same time, the promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam out to the travellers' camp to buy a caravan for the show. Sam came back on a stretcher — a bare-knuckle traveller named Finn had put him down over the price of a wheel — and now Halloway had no fighter for Coldstone's fixed bout. Halloway swallowed hard, put Finn in instead, and promised Coldstone the man would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed that same week, dropped the stone with the fence Hersch, and went straight to the bookmaker's to put money on the fight Grigor had mentioned. Ike, Benno and a fool named Tulley bungled the job badly, snatching Solly's arm — case and all — and running when Grigor himself came roaring in to chase them off, as if he hadn't sent them there himself.

In the ring, Finn ignored every instruction and flattened his man in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and made Halloway feel every penny of it with his fists.

Marv arrived to find Solly gone and hired the bounty hunter Ledge, a man who tracked debts like other men tracked deer. Meanwhile Grigor had Solly in a back room, cutting the arm off at the shoulder to get the case open — only to find the stone wasn't inside it at all.

Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the next fight went wrong too.

Ledge, meanwhile, traced Ike and Benno's car, shot it to pieces on a coast road, and took both men and the stone they'd been carrying.

Halloway and Digby told Finn to go down in the fourth this time — no mistakes. Coldstone's men, to make the point permanent, burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan that same night.

Grigor, still hunting his stone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno inside. The shootout left Ledge, Grigor and Benno all dead in the road, and only Tulley got clean away — with the dog that had swallowed the diamond somewhere back at the start of all this.

The second fight went differently than anyone planned. Finn knocked his man out cold in the fourth exactly as ordered, and then the travellers, waiting in the crowd for what had been done to Finn's mother, tore Coldstone's men apart where they stood.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone hiding in his own office and shot him themselves. By morning the travellers were gone, tents and all, as if they'd never been there.

The dog turned up weeks later at a pet shop, sick and thin, and coughed the diamond onto the floor in front of the astonished owner. It was handed over, eventually, to two tired men who no longer had a fighter, a boss, or the faintest idea what to do with a stone that had cost so many lives to travel so short a distance.

THE DOG

Tigre was born to a rottweiler that Nestor kept chained by the door, and from the beginning the animal killed anything smaller that crossed him. Ruben found out by accident, watching him tear through a neighbor's mutt in seconds, and something in him lit up with an idea. He started entering Tigre in the local fights behind the tannery, and the dog won and won, until Ruben was no longer the household's forgotten younger brother but a man with pockets full of cash and no one to answer to but himself.

The winning didn't last. In a back-alley ring lit by truck headlights, the promoter Chaco, cheated of a bet, put a bullet in Tigre rather than pay out. Ruben stabbed him before he could think about it and ran into the dark with his friend Pipo, the dog left twitching in the sawdust, forgotten in the chaos of men scattering from gunfire.

He was still running, foot to the floor, blood roaring, when he blew through a red light and drove into a stranger's car. The stranger was Celine Vaz, a model whose face hung forty feet tall over the avenue where her lover Hector had installed her, in a flat that stared out at her own billboard smile. Cardo — a vagrant who had once been a guerrilla and was now paid in cash to disappear men quietly — happened to be crossing that same junction. He left the wreck alone but pulled the bleeding dog from the wrong car, some old reflex from years of not looking away from suffering, and carried Tigre off into the dark like a man carrying something he owed a debt to.

The helicopters came at night, low and slow, their blades chopping the fog into ribbons as they crossed over every roof in the city, spraying for the pests that had gotten into the crops that spring. In one of those houses, Neil Hartigan stood in front of a mirror knotting his tie while his wife Bess dabbed paint from under her nails, both of them getting ready for a dinner party they'd been dreading all week.

Across town, Otto Kemp wiped flour from his hands and wrote "Charlie" in careful icing script on his order pad, promising Elaine Rill the cake would be ready by Saturday.

Charlie never made it to the party. On his way to school a waitress named Rhona, late for her shift, took the corner too fast and struck him with her car. He got up, brushed off his jeans, and told his mother he was fine, he just wanted to lie down.

He never woke from that lying down. The coma took him quietly, and his parents Grant and Elaine sat in plastic chairs under fluorescent light for days. Grant's father Duff, a man Grant hadn't spoken to in a decade, appeared in the doorway one evening and confessed, unprompted, to an affair he'd had thirty years before, as if unloading it might save his grandson.

The cake sat unclaimed and unpaid for. Otto, humiliated and broke, began calling the Rills' house late at night, saying nothing, just breathing until they hung up.

Meanwhile Cheryl sat cross-legged on her living room couch, murmuring men's fantasies back to them through the phone while her husband Stu smoked in the doorway, saying nothing, his jaw tight.

Stu went fishing that weekend with three friends, Vern among them, and found a woman floating face down in the shallows. They tied her ankle to a root with fishing line and kept casting for two more days before anyone called it in. Vern's wife Iris, who dressed as a clown for children's birthdays, learned what they'd done and couldn't look at her husband's hands again.

At the club downtown, the singer Vida took the stage every night in sequins while her daughter Bee sat home alone with her cello, playing scales to no one.

Officer Rowe left his family's dog tied to a stranger's fence one afternoon, a small lie to cover a bigger one, on his way to see a woman named Nan who wasn't his wife. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot who flew the very spraying routes over the city at night, heard she'd found someone new and took a saw to her dining table, her chairs, her bed frame, until the apartment looked like a woodshop.

House-sitting for the Hartigans, Ike photographed his girlfriend Dot lying in the hallway with bruise makeup and fake blood, laughing between shots, careless of whose home it was.

The dinner party finally happened, later than planned. Bess, three glasses of wine in, told the table about modeling nude for a painter in her twenties, and then, quieter, about an affair years after that. Neil stood up so fast his chair fell backward.

Charlie died that same week. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery, furious, meaning to shout, but Otto only pulled warm bread from the oven and set it before them, and the three of them sat in the flour dust and cried.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch after another late show and, without waking her, walked to the garage, pulled the door down, and sat in the car with the engine running.

At a picnic in the hills, sun bright on the grass, Stu picked up a stone and brought it down on a young woman's skull while the others looked away too late.

That evening the ground shook, one long tremor rolling under the whole city — cracking Nan's windows, rattling Otto's ovens, tipping Cheryl's phone off its cradle — and by nightfall the news folded it all together: the tremor, the girl in the river, the boy who never woke, the daughter in the garage, one bulletin, one voice, reading it all as if it had happened all at once.

The gun dealer had a way of stretching Nadir's words back at him, flattening the vowels, grinning like he was doing him a favor by selling him the pistol at all. Sahar stood beside her father and said nothing, and it was she who slipped two boxes into her bag, though only one held live rounds.

Detective Isaiah Reece would stand over a body on a shoulder of frozen weeds months later and recognize his brother's shoes before he recognized his face. That was still ahead of everything else here, waiting.

Trey and Kwame took Halstead's car outside the restaurant with the practiced calm of men who had done it before, laughing about it two blocks later like it was nothing, like nothing was coming.

Officer Boyle pulled the Hobarts over on a street with no other witnesses and put his hands on Renee while her husband Clay sat frozen behind the wheel, and later that same week his partner Voss stood in the commander's office and asked, flatly, for a new car, a new partner, anyone else.

Mateo came to change the Halsteads' locks and Paula watched him from the top of the stairs like he was casing the place, said so to his face, and he said nothing, only worked. Days after, he knelt at Nadir's shop door and told him plainly that the frame was rotted through, that the lock alone wouldn't hold, and Nadir called him a thief dressed as a fixer.

The shop was hollowed out overnight — shelves, register, glass — and when Nadir called his insurer, they read him his own signature off the waiver Mateo had made him initial, and refused to pay a cent.

Boyle sat across from Delia Frank with his father's chart in his hands and she slid the folder back to him, unmoved, and there is a version of Boyle, later, thick with smoke, hauling a woman out of an upside-down wreck by her collar, not knowing yet it is Renee Hobart until her face turns to him in the firelight and something in him breaks open at the recognition.

Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham with the stolen car and left him on the curb outside the ER without a backward glance.

Weeks on, Clay would be caught mid-theft of his own repossessed car, surrounded, and it would be Voss again, talking men with guns out of pulling their triggers over a man in his own driveway. Clay would drive off with Trey in the passenger seat, punch the wheel through red lights, and throw him out onto the gravel at the end of it, done with all of it.

Nadir waited in his car outside Mateo's house with the pistol on the seat beside him, and when Mateo came out into the drive his daughter Rosie ran to him, and Nadir fired as she reached his arms. The girl stood untouched, screaming but whole, and Nadir sat there afterward understanding what his own daughter had done for him — bought him blanks, saved him from himself — and he wept and called her his angel.

Voss, alone on a night road, picked up a hitchhiker and read a hand moving toward a pocket as a weapon and fired, then burned the car with the body still in it. The man was Kwame. It was Reece who got the call, who drove to the scattered debris off the shoulder and found what was left of his own brother, and it was Reece's mother, days later, who told him plainly that he had never once gone looking for Kwame while there was still time, and that this was on him, not the road.

Trey, alone now, opened the back of Pham's abandoned van and found it full of trafficked people, silent and terrified, and instead of selling them on he drove them to the docks and let them go into the fog.

Paula fell down her own stairs reaching for a phone she didn't need, and it was Alba who caught her, who she clung to and told, weeping, that she had no one else, no other friend in the world.

The first snow came thin and fast, and two cars met at a corner too quickly, and the drivers stood in the white hush shouting at each other about whose fault it was, as if the city had learned nothing at all.

Emlyn came to Wilder's house the same evening, and Wilder poured him whisky with a hand that would not quite hold steady.

"You'll have heard, then," Wilder said.

"I've heard nothing. Odile telephoned in tears, said something was ended, and then she rang off. I came straight here because it seemed the sort of thing one should do in person." Emlyn settled into the chair he always took, as if the house still belonged partly to him, which perhaps it did. "She let slip, apparently, that I've been publishing a man you represent. The one we both loathe. That seemed to distress her more than anything else."

"She told me last night, in the bar on Culross Street, that it's over between you. That she'd spent the whole of the night before confessing to you — everything, from the beginning."

Emlyn turned his glass in his hand and did not look surprised. "I've known for four years, you understand. She told me on the trip abroad — the hotel, the letter at the desk in your hand, which I recognised at once. I asked her about it and she gave me the whole of it there in the room, very calmly, considering."

Wilder said nothing for a moment. He was thinking of the lunch, the long restaurant lunch two years before that, when he and Emlyn had drunk through three courses and Emlyn had baited him mercilessly about contemporary fiction, about the slackness of modern prose, and never once, not once, mentioned what he must already have known. And the dinner after that, at the house, the two of them talking about racquets and school sport for a solid hour while Odile sat with no part in it at all, as though she were furniture they had agreed between them not to discuss.

"You never said anything," Wilder said. "All that time."

"What was there to say? You were my closest friend. I'd always been fonder of you than of her, if I'm honest — I told her so, that afternoon abroad, and it seemed to settle something in her, oddly. She went back to your rooms afterward and said nothing whatever about the trip. I know because I asked her once, much later, and she said the afternoon had passed exactly as all the others had. Linen, plates, that ordinary domestic silence you'd built between you."

Wilder remembered the rooms in the quiet district, the linen and plates they had bought together as though playing at a marriage, the whole small household of it. He remembered when Odile had said she was carrying her husband's child and they had agreed, gravely, that nothing between them would change — that the rooms would go on exactly as before. And they had, for a while. Then the rooms became a chore, the crockery got split between them without much ceremony, the lease surrendered, and that had seemed the end of it, until the bar two years later when she'd told him her marriage was over.

"And your letters," Emlyn said, almost gently, "I never thought much of them either, if we're totting things up honestly tonight."

"I never sent you any of the good ones."

"No. I don't suppose you did."

They sat with that a while, two men who had discussed sport for an hour rather than say a true word to each other, who had drunk through lunches instead. Wilder thought of the upstairs room at his own party, years and years back now, where he'd first led her away from the noise of the other guests and told her, with the particular sincerity of a man half-drunk on his own charm, how lovely she was. It seemed a very long way from this room, this chair, this friend who had known everything for four years and said nothing, and who now simply finished his whisky and stood, and put on his coat, and left without any further explanation, as though the matter, having been so long carried, required no more words to be finally set down.

All moments, Billy learned, are stitched together simultaneously, and so he found no particular reason to tell about them in the order they occurred. He told me about the zoo first—the pink dome on the alien planet, the film actress lounging on the couch across from him, the crowds of glowing eyes pressed to the glass. The aliens told him that free will was a parochial notion, that every instant already existed, fixed and gleaming like a bead on a wire, and he believed them completely, because by then nothing in his life had ever happened in an order that made sense to him anyway.

He told me about being born next, though he said it the way you'd mention weather from a country you'd once visited. Small industrial town. Weak lungs. A peculiar quiet child who didn't cry so much as observe. And then, without any transition, the pool—his father's hands under his arms, the heave, the water closing over him, the sinking that felt less like drowning than like being filed away in a drawer.

He was shot, he told me, exactly as he'd always known he would be, on a stage after a speech about the fourth dimension, a beam of light finding him mid-sentence. He said this in the same breath as describing his daughter's face when she decided he was senile and took the checkbook and the car keys and the house out of his name. He did not seem bothered by either. He said the assassination and the daughter's decision existed at the same time as his childhood, at the same time as the war, at the same time as everything.

The war he described in pieces that refused to link. The chaplain's assistant posting, shipped overseas with no training worth mentioning. The scout who beat him in a forest for wanting to lie down and die. The scout's death on the prison train, gangrene climbing his leg, blaming Billy with his final rancid breath. The camp beside enemy officers drawing double rations for years through a clerical error nobody had bothered to correct. The great city, the meat locker they were housed in, the fire that took the whole place in a single night so that when the prisoners climbed up the city simply wasn't there anymore. The digging afterward, the corpses in the cellars, a man dying of the dry heaves from the smell alone. A different prisoner, later or earlier, promising to have him killed one day for the scout's sake, a debt that never seemed to come due on any schedule Billy could name.

Somewhere in all this—he was never sure where, and neither was I—he came home and collapsed and was hospitalized, and there met a hack science fiction writer another patient introduced him to, a man full of theories about time and space that Billy found he already agreed with before he'd finished hearing them. He married the daughter of the optometry school's owner and became rich, though he told this part flatly, as though wealth were just another room he'd once stood in. He survived a plane crash in the mountains—he was almost cheerful about it—and his wife died afterward of exhaust fumes in the car on the way to see him at the hospital, which he mentioned and then moved past, the way you'd step over a crack in a sidewalk.

He went on the radio once to tell everyone about the aliens and the zoo and the fourth dimension, and no one believed him, and this didn't trouble him either, because he'd already told me he would be shot for saying such things, and he had already been shot, and he was already a child sinking to the bottom of a pool, and he was already an old man boarding a stage he had boarded a thousand times before.

He said it all so calmly. He said there was no order to any of it worth insisting on. He said the moment is structured that way.

He was shot, he told me, exactly as he'd always known he would be, on a stage after a speech about the fourth dimension, a beam of light finding him mid-sentence. He said this in the same breath as describing his daughter's face when she decided he was senile and took the checkbook and the car keys and the house out of his name. He did not seem bothered by either. He said the assassination and the daughter's decision existed at the same time as his childhood, at the same time as the war, at the same time as everything.

The war he described in pieces that refused to link. The chaplain's assistant posting, shipped overseas with no training worth mentioning. The scout who beat him in a forest for wanting to lie down and die. The scout's death on the prison train, gangrene climbing his leg, blaming Billy with his final rancid breath. The camp beside enemy officers drawing double rations for years through a clerical error nobody had bothered to correct. The great city, the meat locker they were housed in, the fire that took the whole place in a single night so that when the prisoners climbed up the city simply wasn't there anymore. The digging afterward, the corpses in the cellars, a man dying of the dry heaves from the smell alone. A different prisoner, later or earlier, promising to have him killed one day for the scout's sake, a debt that never seemed to come due on any schedule Billy could name.

Somewhere in all this—he was never sure where, and neither was I—he came home and collapsed and was hospitalized, and there met a hack science fiction writer another patient introduced him to, a man full of theories about time and space that Billy found he already agreed with before he'd finished hearing them. He married the daughter of the optometry school's owner and became rich, though he told this part flatly, as though wealth were just another room he'd once stood in. He survived a plane crash in the mountains—he was almost cheerful about it—and his wife died afterward of exhaust fumes in the car on the way to see him at the hospital, which he mentioned and then moved past, the way you'd step over a crack in a sidewalk.

He went on the radio once to tell everyone about the aliens and the zoo and the fourth dimension, and no one believed him, and this didn't trouble him either, because he'd already told me he would be shot for saying such things, and he had already been shot, and he was already a child sinking to the bottom of a pool, and he was already an old man boarding a stage he had boarded a thousand times before.

He said it all so calmly. He said there was no order to any of it worth insisting on. He said the moment is structured that way.
